sm: On November 30, the Supreme Court will hear argument on whether school employees can sue under Title IX, which bars sex discrimination by federally funded schools, or must rely on Title VII of the Civil Rights Act. The plaintiffs are Thomas Crowther, a former art professor at Augusta University who lost his contract after student misconduct accusations, and Machelle Joseph, the fired Georgia Tech women's basketball coach who had complained about unequal resources. The 11th Circuit held Title IX gives employees no right to sue. The employees point to Title IX's broad text, its narrow exceptions that omit employment, the 1982 North Haven decision, and past rulings allowing employment suits under Title VI and the Rehabilitation Act. The Georgia university system agrees Title IX bars employment discrimination but says the question is whether employees may sue privately.

The university system argues the Supreme Court has only assumed, never held, that Title VI allows employment suits. It adds that the Rehabilitation Act is more detailed, and that North Haven did not address a private remedy. It contends that Congress extended Title VII's detailed enforcement scheme to school employees weeks before passing Title IX, so a second right to sue would be an inexplicable about-face. It also notes that Title IX suits would skip Title VII requirements such as filing first with the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission and its damage limits. Crowther and Joseph reply that the two laws are vastly different and that Congress enacted overlapping remedies. The university system further invokes the Spending Clause and last term's Landor decision, saying funding recipients must knowingly agree to extra sanctions like private suits.

Crowther and Joseph respond that funding recipients have been on notice of private suits for intentional sex discrimination since 1979. West Virginia and twenty other states, in a friend of the court brief, say the deal they accepted did not include these suits and that Title VII was the proper route. The Trump administration, through Solicitor General D. John Sauer, supports the university but urges the justices to decide on statutory interpretation alone and avoid the Spending Clause question. The administration and the National School Attorneys Association warn that a ruling for the employees would crowd court dockets and burden school districts with limited staff. The National Education Association counters that upholding the 11th Circuit would remove a deterrent against mistreatment of educators and that Title VII does not fully protect them. A decision is expected by late June or early July.
